analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and Florida straits.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Energy Committee since April 2025 with no hearing or vote; all 16 cosponsors are Democrats or independents.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into law against selling or allowing oil and gas drilling on the federal ocean floor off the Atlantic coast — from New England to Florida — and in the Straits of Florida. It covers the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas, the same zones the federal government outlined in its 2024-2029 leasing program. No drilling is happening in most of these waters now, so the bill would foreclose it before it starts.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, beachgoers, and the tourism economies of Atlantic and Gulf-adjacent states gain protection from oil spill risk, which can shut down beaches and fisheries for years. Commercial and recreational fishing operations avoid the risk of contaminated waters. States that rely on clean coastlines keep their main economic asset off-limits to drilling leases.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or other minerals in four Atlantic planning areas.
The ban is written to override any other provision of the leasing law, so a future administration could not open these waters by administrative action; only a new act of Congress could reverse it.
The protected areas cover the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, and South Atlantic planning areas and the Straits of Florida, matching the zones identified in the 2024-2029 federal leasing program.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies give up any future access to Atlantic offshore leases. The federal treasury forgoes potential royalty revenue from any drilling that would otherwise occur, and the country forgoes whatever domestic production those areas might eventually have supplied — though these waters currently host little or no producing offshore drilling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and federal royalties

drawbacks.text: The ban permanently removes potential future domestic energy supply and the federal royalty income it could generate, which supporters of Atlantic drilling argue weakens energy security and forecloses economic development that coastal states might want to choose for themselves.

Because the prohibition applies permanently and overrides other provisions of law, it takes the decision away from future administrations and future coastal governors and legislatures, whatever conditions might then prevail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but preventive: these Atlantic areas are not producing oil today, so the bill blocks a risk that does not yet exist rather than fixing an existing harm. The cost is foregone access and royalties for industry and the treasury in an area where commercial drilling has never taken hold. The main honest tradeoff is permanence — locking the decision in for all future conditions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by 13 Senate Democrats and both independents as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on April 10, 2025.
Sixteen senators in total — 14 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both independents — are listed as cosponsors; no Republican has signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the oil and gas industry keeps its option open: with no vote, Atlantic waters remain nominally available for leasing, and no drilling ban exists in law. Nothing has been decided yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the status quo — drilling option stays open

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act and recruited 13 Democratic and both independent cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing or markup scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat or independent (14 of 45 Democrats, both independents); no Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats and chair the committee the bill sits in.

industries.note: The bill permanently bars leasing for oil, gas, and mineral development in four Atlantic planning areas, removing future access the industry could otherwise compete for. Coastal communities would bear the spill risk while companies and the treasury would capture the revenue, which is why the industry's interest runs against the coastal public here.
Beach towns and resort economies depend on clean coastlines; an oil spill can close beaches and cost a season's revenue, so a permanent drilling ban protects their core asset.
Fishing grounds off the Atlantic coast would be shielded from drilling platforms, seismic surveys, and spill contamination that can close fisheries for years.

analysis.trajectory: With a 55-45 Republican majority, a Republican chair of the Energy Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a vote this Congress. Similar Atlantic-drilling ban bills have been introduced for years and have died in committee; the realistic outcome is that it sits until the session ends unless control of the Senate or the committee agenda changes.
